newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE-Turtles thrive under Cyprus project.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Turtles thrive under Cyprus project.

text.p: A small nondescript sign, grey from the billows of dust which have settled over it during the summer, directs visitors along a potholed track through packs of mountain goats and sheep to a sandy cove.

The Lara beach is about one kilometre long on the western coast of Cyprus in the unspoilt Akamas peninsula, an area with deep gorges and spectacular coast, and home to the only turtle conservation project in the Mediterranean.

The words "turtle hatchery" instantly conjure up images of a beach -- and its sea -- crawling with reptiles, big and small. Not so, according to Andreas Demetropoulos, director of Cyprus's fisheries department.
In fact, he says, turtles are so shy that people are banned from walking the beaches at night. In daytime turtles are nowhere to be found.
"During the day bathers are not a problem," Demetropoulos told Reuters. "We just don't want them here at night because that is when everything happens."
Between June and August groups of female turtles crawl onto the beach at night to lay their eggs, which hatch seven weeks later.
Turtles' privacy is safeguarded by a ban on development and a dirt road full of potholes guaranteed to dampen the vigour of any daredevil driver.
Over-development has turned turtles away from many other beaches on the island, but some still occasionally turn up on hotel beaches, attracted by the bright lights.
"We recently got a call from one hotel that turtles were crawling up its lawns," said Demetropoulos.
Lara is one of the last nesting sites in the region of the green turtle and the loggerhead turtle, both endangered species. In the entire Mediterranean, only 500 to 1000 adults are left.
The first turtle nests were discovered in Cyprus in the early 1970s.
"We actually found the first nests on this beach here, people thought there were none left," said Demetropoulos, adding that their exploitation in Europe made the population collapse.

By 1978 a comprehensive government programme started on their conservation. This includes tagging adult turtles to keep track of the population, marking nests and covering them with wired cages with gaps large enough for the hatchlings to get out. Occasionally nests are moved if they risk being destroyed by waves.
The fisheries department also holds training courses in hatchery techniques and beach management for Mediterranean scientists each year, sponsored by the United Nations Environment Programme.

Around 100 female turtles nest in Lara and other nearby beaches every three to five years, laying a cluster of about 80 eggs every two weeks between June and August. Last year around 8,000 hatchlings were released from Cyprus's shores.
"Those are babies, just a few hours old," says Demetropoulos, pointing to a blue water cooler in the corner of a wooden shed.
Tiny green turtles, slightly larger than a baby's hand, were climbing over one another, their eyes barely open.
"The other eggs hatched this morning. We had to dig into the sand to find these ones, they were the leftovers," said Demtropoulos, holding a tiny turtle in his palm.
Turtles lay in the sand because it provides a steady temperature for the hatchlings. The sex ratio of the hatchlings also changes with the depth the egg is laid at and the temperature.
The probability the turtle will be a male rises when the egg is laid deeper, where the temperature is colder. The top batch of eggs are inevitably females, where temperatures are warmer.
"We can play God, yes," said Demetropoulos, as though anticipating the question. "But we don't want to. We do things the natural way."
Later that evening the turtles were left on the beach to make their own way into the sea, attracted by the moonlight reflection off the blue waters.
It is a precarious journey for the hour-old reptiles and not all of them will survive. Crabs on the beach, foxes lurking in the hills above and sea predators are waiting for them.

Between 15 and 30 years from now those females which will survive will return to Lara to lay their eggs. "They imprint," Demetropoulos explains. "They recognise the beach they were laid on and they will always return to that one. They are very selective."
